newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan problem loans no longer massive - MOF official.
newsitem.headline: Japan problem loans no longer massive - MOF official.

text.p: The amount of problem loans at Japan's deposit-taking financial institutions as a whole shrank from March through September and is no longer massive, a senior Ministry of Finance (MOF) official said on Thursday.

While uncovered loan losses are estimated at 7.3 trillion yen, this is similar to the 7.86 trillion yen in operating profits expected at financial institutions in the business year to next March, he told a news conference, implying that the institutions have the wherewithal to deal with the current level of problem loans.

Earlier on Thursday, MOF announced that Japan's deposit-taking financial institutions including small credit unions and agricultural financial firms had 29.23 trillion yen in problem loans -- bad loans to bankrupt firms, non-performing loans in which interest payments are in arrears for six months or more and restructuring loans -- at the end of September.
This was down from 34.80 trillion yen in problem loans and 8.31 trillion yen in uncovered loan losses at the end of March.
The amount of problem loans at the end of September excluded loans to failed "jusen" mortgage firms, a MOF official said.

Japan's 20 biggest banks held 17.41 trillion yen in problem loans, MOF said in a statement. Annual operating profits for the 20 banks averaged 4.81 trillion yen in the five years through 1995/96, ended March 31.
Unrealised profits at all deposit-taking institutions totalled 23.51 trillion yen at the end of September, of which the 20 biggest banks had 16.11 trillion yen, MOF said in its statement.
